SnapDragon (bred as NY1) was developed by Susan Brown at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a 1998 cross of Honeycrisp and the advanced Cornell selection NY 752, reaching commercial release in 2013 alongside its sibling RubyFrost after about a decade of evaluation. It ripens in early-to-mid fall, ahead of RubyFrost, and is prized for an extremely crisp, dense bite along with a sweet flavor carrying a distinctive spicy note inherited from its Honeycrisp parent. It is best suited to the cold-winter apple regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that the Geneva breeding program targets, and it stores well under refrigeration, though not as long as the later-ripening RubyFrost.

RubyFrost (bred as NY2) was developed by Susan Brown at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a cross of Braeburn and Autumn Crisp, taking roughly seventeen years to reach commercial release in 2013 alongside its sibling SnapDragon. It ripens late in the season, after SnapDragon, and is notable for unusually high vitamin C content along with firm, dense flesh and a tangy-sweet flavor that holds up exceptionally well in cold storage, often keeping quality for months. It is best suited to the cold-winter apple regions of the Northeast and Upper Midwest that the Geneva breeding program targets, and its thick skin and dense texture also resist bruising during handling.

Developed by David Bedford and James Luby at the University of Minnesota from a cross of Honeycrisp and the University of Arkansas selection AA44, this cultivar (breeding number MN55) was selected in the late 1990s and released commercially by Stemilt Growers in 2017 under the trade name Rave, while fruit grown within Minnesota is marketed separately as First Kiss. It is one of the earliest-ripening apples in the Honeycrisp lineage, typically ready in mid-to-late August, several weeks before Honeycrisp itself, while sharing a similarly crisp, juicy texture and sweet-tart flavor. Because it ripens over an extended window, growers often pick over the tree in multiple passes rather than in one harvest, and it suits the cold winters of the Upper Midwest that the University of Minnesota breeding program targets.

Triumph (breeding number MN80) was selected in 2004 by the University of Minnesota apple breeding program from a 1990 cross of Honeycrisp and Liberty, and it was released to nurseries starting in 2021 after extensive evaluation for disease resistance. It carries two distinct genetic sources of resistance to apple scab along with low-to-moderate susceptibility to cedar apple rust, making it well suited to organic growers and low-spray home orchards. Fruit ripens in late September, around the same time as or slightly after Honeycrisp, with attractive coloring and occasional russeting near the stem, and the tree is confirmed hardy to USDA zone 4.
